extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, Federal Social Security Tribunal Secretariat, UIC (Unemployment Insurance Commission) officials, members/chairmen of Boards of referees
extracted.subtask_description: Recommendations and procedural standards for the operation, training, decision-writing, appeals jurisdiction, and overpayment recovery practices of a Federal Social Security Tribunal and Boards of referees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing scheduling and notice requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for when hearings are to be granted and how notice is given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An appellant may apply in writing to the Tribunal for a hearing within fifteen days of docket filing and the Tribunal shall grant a hearing. The Tribunal may at any time direct that there shall be a hearing. At least fourteen days prior to the hearing a notice in writing shall be given by the Tribunal to (a) the appellant, (b) the Commission, and (c) any other person or association having immediate interest or whom the Tribunal deems expedient to notify. The procedure at the hearing shall be determined by the Tribunal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written decisions with statement of reasons and distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions must be in writing and include reasons, with copies sent to interested parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A decision of the Tribunal shall be in writing and shall contain a statement of reasons, and a copy shall be sent to the appellant, the Commission, and any other person or association having an immediate interest or whom the Tribunal deems expedient to notify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Tribunal appeal jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Scope of matters the Federal Social Security Tribunal should hear on appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeal jurisdiction should not be limited to benefits or unemployment insurance but encompass benefits and contributions for all federal social security schemes (unemployment insurance, Canada Pension Plan, Old Age Security, family allowances) and potentially veterans' pensions and allowances; in most cases the Tribunal will be a second-level appeal after an initial level established by the scheme Acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision quality and reliance on training
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of tribunal/board decisions must be sufficiently high and depends on training when decision-makers are not professional judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For tribunals composed of 'amateurs' (e.g., Boards of referees) the quality of decisions depends to a large extent on special training received. The product of the operation must be of high quality to exert moral authority over parties; training and writing standards are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial training documentation and Manual of Procedure contents
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific materials and procedural guidance that initial training should provide and that the Tribunal's Manual should contain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documentation to be provided to new members should include: (1) text of the Act and Regulations; (2) a Manual of Procedure describing Board procedures and Tribunal guidelines on stages such as when the chairman should summon parties, joinder of appeals, content of the chairman's introductory statement, length of hearing, procedure for examining and cross-examining parties, recording and retention of discussions, clerk participation, Board deliberations, form and writing of majority/minority decisions, role of interpreters, importance attached to UIC internal criteria for assessing claims, and extent of the Board's jurisdiction with regard to summaries of the file. The manual should be designed for constant referral and kept up to date by the Tribunal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance and accessibility of training materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuals and training materials must be kept current and accessible for frequent referral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Manual of Procedure should be organized so members can constantly refer to it; the Tribunal is responsible for keeping it up to date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to caselaw, digests and indexes
rubrics_metrics.description: Members must have access to tribunal decisions, digests and indexing to support consistent application of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide collected decisions (e.g., of the Umpire and the Tribunal), supplemented by a detailed alphabetical index by subject; members should receive Tribunal decisions dealing with unemployment insurance quickly, with notes from the Secretariat and be on the mailing list for official reports of the Tribunal's caselaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of claimant and UIC documentation to members
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure members and hearing rooms have access to claimant-facing materials and UIC internal documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the claimant's manual and make UIC internal documentation (UIC Manual, UIC Guidelines, Medical Yardsticks, Labour Market Statistics) permanently available in the hearing room and kept up to date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing training and seminar frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Ongoing professional development requirements for Board members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuing training should be based on the Manual of Procedure, the synopsis of the scheme, and caselaw reports; delivered via periodic conferences and seminars (at least two per year) organized and led by the Tribunal Secretariat with UIC senior management and Tribunal members participating. Members should be informed of local Tribunal hearings and encouraged to attend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of assignments and rotation to ensure experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure sufficient on-the-job experience through assignment frequency and panel rotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fix the number of Board members so that each chairman could, in theory, sit at least 25 times a year and each employer/employee representative at least 20 times a year to foster on-the-job training. Explain these requirements clearly to prospective candidates. The principle of rotation within panels helps but volume of appeals varies and must be accounted for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-writing standards and decision form
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for content, organization, terminology and style of Board decisions and provision of a decision form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tribunal should develop a decision form to facilitate enumeration of factual conclusions, statement of applicable legal rules (legislation and caselaw), and an account of the solution to the litigation. The Manual should contain specific information on organization, terminology and style to be used in decisions. Regional seminars (perhaps every two years) for chairmen should be organized to discuss difficulties in writing decisions, including case studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording and transcription of hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Record proceedings to permit transcription and to improve decision content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record entire proceedings (e.g., on tape) so they can be transcribed in the event of an appeal; this allows Boards to limit factual accounts in writing and elaborate legal reasoning and solutions, improving the information value of decisions despite tight time constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of considering undue hardship before recovery action
rubrics_metrics.description: Overpayment recovery decisions should account for the claimant's capacity and potential undue hardship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because unemployment insurance aims to help people through periods of unemployment, UIC should assess recovery possibilities for their effect on overpayment 'debtors' and choose another method if undue hardship is a possibility. The Act allows write-off where recovery would cause undue hardship; UIC should consider hardship before initiating recovery action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor recovery methods to cause of overpayment
rubrics_metrics.description: Select recovery method based on whether the overpayment was caused by UIC, claimant misrepresentation, negligence, or shared responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate overpayments caused by UIC, claimants, or both. For UIC-caused overpayments seek voluntary repayment or write-off; reserve harsh methods (garnishment, Federal Court) for individuals who caused overpayments willfully or negligently and have refused voluntary repayment schedules. The UIC's present practice of treating overpayments uniformly is criticized and should be reformed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility for payment delays and notice timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept and account for internal payment delays to avoid unfair overpayments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some overpayments occur because of delay between a decision ending payment and actual cessation of cheque issuance/mailing. The UIC should accept the burden of such delays; effective end time should be when a payment centre learns and acts to stop issuance. Consider producing notices from Regional Payment Centres to ensure internal communication delays don't cause overpayments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and limits of recoupment and tax reversal
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit automatic use of recoupment and tax reversal; inform claimants and prefer recovery of net amounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recoupment and tax reversal are administratively attractive but potentially harmful if automatic. Delay recoupment (e.g., two-week delay policy is an improvement) and ensure claimants know the purpose and how to negotiate reduced recoupment. Consider ceasing tax reversal except where people consent with a full understanding of consequences. Recover net amounts only (not gross) and negotiate with the Department of National Revenue to recover tax deducted at source where appropriate. Ensure claimants are informed of partial recoupment options and a national policy on appropriate levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions and justification for garnishment and Federal Court actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit severe recovery methods to clearly justified cases and require proof of fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Garnishment and Federal Court action should be restricted to situations where the person affected has recognizable responsibility for the overpayment and undue hardship will not be caused. Require the Commission to justify Federal Court use by showing the person was 'at fault' and had been convicted under the Act or had admitted awareness of receipt of monies not entitled to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation periods for recovery: absolute and unalterable
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory time limits for recovery should be respected and not circumvented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Act prescribes time limits for recovery (three years normally, six years if fraud/misrepresentation). The UIC should not seek to overcome these by voluntary repayment agreements or waivers of limitation periods; limitation periods should be viewed as absolute legislative constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for 'undue hardship' write-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Refine, publicize and apply consistent criteria for when overpayments should be written off on grounds of undue hardship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation of 'undue hardship' varies; criteria found were often narrower. While allowing flexibility and personal consideration, the Commission should refine and publicize criteria so officials exercise discretion knowledgeably and reasonably. Criteria should not be rigid nor mechanical but should encourage fair, informed decision-making beyond minimal factors like permanent disability or age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information and communication to claimants about overpayments and repayment options
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate clearly and simply to affected persons about overpayment determinations, recovery methods, and available remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UIC's present practice does not clearly inform claimants whether instalment repayment plans exist or how to negotiate partial deductions. Communications should set out options in simple language. The approach to overpayment recovery should include better information for affected persons, including their appeal rights and ability to negotiate reduced recoupment or partial repayment schedules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of appellate review of overpayment amounts and interaction with appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify how overpayment determinations interact with appeals and what appellate tribunals may/cannot do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is confusing that an overpayment determination cannot by itself be appealed to a Board of referees and Umpires; these appellate tribunals cannot vary the amount of an overpayment although they can review related issues. Procedures and information about appeals as a remedy against overpayment determination or recovery should be clarified for claimants.
